surfaces.part: stone stair treads (alternating light tread and darker riser bands)

answer.evidence: The staircase has repeating light tread bands of about 3 rows (30-32, 36-38, 42-44, 48-50, 56-60). Each tread sits above a darker 3-row riser (33-35, 39-41, 45-47, 51-53), and a dark edge line at row 29 sits above the first light tread. This reads as horizontal tread surfaces seen from above with vertical risers below them, not a flat elevation. The treads are foreshortened and each is only 3 rows. The arch and the wall blocks are drawn as front faces, which is normal for a wall piece. No isometric side face is visible; the right-hand post is a vertical rail.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate shows 9 visible tones per tile. That matches the hedge but is well below the stall (17) and the well (20), which are the closest structural references. Flat coverage is low at 7%, so there are no large flat fills, and the stone blocks and steps do carry some grain. The stone ramp has only about 4 lightness steps, against 5-6 on the references. 99% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, so the dark outline and the arch opening read as a near-black line with no tint of the adjacent stone. That is the 'sticker' look rather than the material-tone edges the references use. The torch and the chain are thin and sparse, and the whole piece reads as a flatter grey mass than the stall or well. Overall it is a bit shallower than the references, with a neutral outline and a shallow ramp.

surfaces.part: stair treads (lighter bands alternating with darker risers), steps rising into the arch
dark arched opening in wall with top ledge

answer.evidence: The stairs show repeated 3-row lighter treads (rows 30-32, 36-38, 42-44, 48-50), each followed by a 3-row darker riser (33-35, 39-41, 45-47, 51-53), with a dark edge line at row 29 and row 54. The treads get lighter toward the viewer. This is a stepped surface seen from above with front risers. The landing at rows 55-60 is also a lighter tread over a front face. The arch above is a vertical wall opening with a ledge at rows 16-19 and dark interior. Each step has a 3-row tread and a 3-row riser, so the stairs read as three-quarter, not flat front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone stair going up into a dark arched wall opening, with a torch at the upper left. It has about 4 grey steps on the stone (light, mid, dark, deep), against about 5-6 steps per material in the references. Its dark edge pixels are 99% near-neutral, so the outline is a neutral black/grey line rather than a dark tone of the adjacent material. The references with real tinted outlines (hedge 0%, cheese stall 1%) lean toward the material colour. The lamp reference is also neutral, but it is a thin metal pole. Texture is present: stone block seams and speckles, with only 7% near-flat coverage. Visible tones per tile are 9, equal to the hedge but well below the cheese stall (17) and the well (20). The stairs and wall carry fewer distinct tones and are mostly mid-grey with a uniform dark outline, which gives a sticker-like feel next to the richer references. The neutral grey outline and the shallower ramp are the deciding weaknesses.

surfaces.part: side stone wall blocks and arch frame

answer.evidence: The staircase climbs into a dark arched opening. Each step is a light tread band of about 3 rows (24-26, 30-32, 36-38, 42-44, 48-50) over a darker riser band of about 3 rows, separated by dark edge lines at rows 29 and 54. The treads widen toward the bottom (silhouette 48 down to 36 and below), which reads as steps seen from above. The wall blocks on either side are vertical stone faces drawn front-on, with no part sticking out that would need its own top face. The stairs read as 3/4 view, though each tread is thin.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a grey stone staircase leading into a dark arch, with a torch on the left and a chain on the right. The stone ramp has about 4 steps (light, mid, dark, deep), against about 5-6 per material in the references. The dark edges and arch outline are almost colourless, with 99% near-neutral dark edge pixels. Only the tinted references (hedge 0%, cheese 1%) lean towards a material tone, so this reads as the near-black sticker-style line rather than a dark tone of the stone. Visible tones per tile are 9, equal to the hedge but well below the well (20) and the cheese stall (17), and the stone faces show little per-block speckle or grain. Near-flat coverage is low at 7%, so large flat fills are not a problem. Overall the piece is shallower than the stall and well on shading depth and outline craft, so it fails on a doubtful call.

surfaces.part: stair treads (alternating light tread, darker riser, steps rising into the arch)

answer.evidence: The stairs show repeating bands in the column scan at x=24 and x=12. Each light tread band is 3 rows (30-32, 36-38, 42-44, 48-50, 56-60) and sits above a darker 3-row riser (33-35, 39-41, 45-47, 51-53). Together these read as treads seen from above with the risers as front faces, and the flight rises toward the dark arch. The wall around it is a vertical face, which is acceptable for a wall piece. The torch is decor. There is no isometric side face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone stair block leading up into a dark arch, with a torch at the left. It shows about 9 visible tones per tile, which matches prop-hedge but is well below prop-well-roofed (20) and prop-stall-cheese (17). Near-flat coverage is 7%, which is low, so large flat fills are not a problem. The stone steps and wall carry some block shading and speckle, but each material ramp is only about 4 steps against the references' 5-6. The main weakness is the outline: 99% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, and by eye the arch opening and step edges are traced in neutral black/dark grey, not in a darker tint of the neighbouring stone. That is the sticker-like look the Beodeul references avoid (the hedge has 0% neutral edge pixels, the stall 1%). The stairs also read as fairly uniform grey blocks with little per-stone variation. Taken together, the neutral outline, the shallower ramps and the lower density than the richer references mean it would look thinner next to them.
